{{Short description|Equation}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''N''-slit interferometric equation}}
[[Quantum mechanics]] was first applied to [[optics]], and [[Interference (wave propagation)|interference]] in particular, by [[Paul Dirac]].<ref name="Dirac">{{cite book|author-link=Paul Dirac |first=P. A. M. |last=Dirac |title=The Principles of Quantum Mechanics |edition=4th |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |location=London |date=1978 |isbn=978-0-19-851208-0}}{{page needed|date=October 2017}}</ref> [[Richard Feynman]], in his [[The Feynman Lectures on Physics|Lectures on Physics]], uses Dirac's notation to describe [[thought experiment]]s on [[double-slit interference]] of [[electron]]s.<ref>{{cite book|author-link=Richard Feynman |first1=R. P. |last1=Feynman |first2=R. B. |last2=Leighton |first3=M. |last3=Sands |title=The Feynman Lectures on Physics |volume=III |publisher=[[Addison Wesley]] |location=Reading |date=1965}}{{page needed|date=October 2017}}</ref> Feynman's approach was extended to '''{{mvar|N}}-slit interferometers''' for either single-photon illumination, or narrow-[[linewidth]] [[laser]] illumination, that is, illumination by indistinguishable [[photon]]s, by [[F. J. Duarte|Frank Duarte]].<ref name="D1989">{{Cite journal|author-link=F. J. Duarte |first1=F. J. |last1=Duarte |first2=D. J. |last2=Paine |title=Quantum mechanical description of {{mvar|N}}-slit interference phenomena |journal=Lasers '88; Proceedings of the International Conference |editor1-first=R. C. |editor1-last=Sze |editor2-first=F. J. |editor2-last=Duarte  |publisher=STS |location=McLean, VA|date=1989 |pages=42–47 |bibcode=1989lase.conf...42D}}</ref><ref name="HPDL">{{cite book|author-link=F. J. Duarte |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |contribution=Chapter 2. Dispersive dye lasers |title=High Power Dye Lasers |editor-first=F. J. |editor-last=Duarte |publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] |location=Berlin |date=1991 |isbn=978-3-540-54066-3}}</ref> The {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometer was first applied in the generation and measurement of complex [[interference pattern]]s.<ref name="D1989"/><ref name="HPDL"/>

In this article the generalized {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric equation, derived via Dirac's notation, is described. Although originally derived to reproduce and predict {{mvar|N}}-slit interferograms,<ref name="D1989"/><ref name="HPDL"/> this equation also has applications to other areas of optics.

==Probability amplitudes and the ''{{mvar|N}}''-slit interferometric equation==
[[File:FJ DUARTE-N SLIT INTERFEROMETER.jpg|600px|thumb|right|Top view schematics of the [[N-slit interferometer|{{mvar|N}}-slit interferometer]] indicating the position of the planes {{mvar|s}}, {{mvar|j}}, and {{mvar|x}}. The {{mvar|N}}-slit array, or grating, is positioned at {{mvar|j}}. The intra interferometric distance can be several-hundred meters long. TBE is a telescopic beam expander, MPBE is a multiple-prism [[beam expander]].]]

In this approach the [[probability amplitude]] for the propagation of a photon from a source {{mvar|s}} to an interference plane {{mvar|x}}, via an array of slits {{mvar|j}}, is given using Dirac's [[bra–ket notation]] as<ref name="D1989"/>

:<math> \langle x | s \rangle = \sum_{j=1}^\N \langle x | j \rangle \langle j | s \rangle</math>

This equation represents the probability amplitude of a photon propagating from {{mvar|s}} to {{mvar|x}} via an array of {{mvar|j}} slits. Using a wavefunction representation for probability amplitudes,<ref name="Dirac"/> and defining the probability amplitudes as<ref name="D1989"/><ref name="HPDL"/><ref name="D1993">{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |title=On a generalized interference equation and interferometric measurements |journal=Opt. Commun. |volume=103 |issue=1–2 |pages=8–14 |date=1993 |doi=10.1016/0030-4018(93)90634-H |bibcode=1993OptCo.103....8D}}</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}
\langle j | s \rangle &= \Psi\left(r_{j,s}\right) e^{-i \theta _j} \\
\langle x | j \rangle &= \Psi\left(r_{x,j}\right) e^{-i \phi _j}
\end{align}</math>
 
where {{mvar|θ<sub>j</sub>}} and {{mvar|Φ<sub>j</sub>}} are the incidence and diffraction phase angles, respectively. Thus, the overall probability amplitude can be rewritten as

:<math> \langle x | s \rangle = \sum_{j=1}^N \Psi\left(r_j\right) e^{-i \Omega _j}</math>

where

:<math> \Psi \left(r_j\right) = \Psi\left(r_{x,j}\right) \Psi\left(r_{j,s}\right)</math>

and

:<math> \Omega_j = \theta_j+\phi_j</math>

after some algebra, the corresponding probability becomes<ref name="D1989"/><ref name="HPDL"/><ref name="D1993"/>

:<math> \big|\langle x | s \rangle\big|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^N \Psi\left(r_j\right)^2 +2 \sum_{j=1}^N \Psi\left(r_j\right)\left(\sum_{m=j+1}^N \Psi\left(r_m\right)\cos\left(\Omega_m-\Omega_j\right)\right) </math>

where {{mvar|N}} is the total number of slits in the array, or transmission grating, and the term in parentheses represents the phase that is directly related to the exact path differences derived from the geometry of the {{mvar|N}}-slit array ({{mvar|j}}), the intra interferometric distance, and the interferometric plane {{mvar|x}}.<ref name="D1993"/> In its simplest version, the phase term can be related to the geometry using

:<math>\cos(\Omega_m-\Omega_j) = \cos k |L_{m}-L_{m-1}| </math>

where {{mvar|k}} is the [[wavenumber]], and {{mvar|L<sub>m</sub>}} and {{math|''L''<sub>''m'' − 1</sub>}} represent the exact path differences. Here the [[Paul Dirac|Dirac]]–[[F. J. Duarte|Duarte]] (DD) ''interferometric equation'' is a probability distribution that is related to the intensity distribution measured experimentally.<ref name="D2004">{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |title=Comment on 'Reflection, refraction, and multislit interference' |journal=Eur. J. Phys. |volume=25 |issue=5 |page=L57–L58 |date=2004 |doi=10.1088/0143-0807/25/5/L04 |bibcode=2004EJPh...25L..57D|s2cid=250829486 }}</ref> The calculations are performed numerically.<ref name="D1993"/>

The DD interferometric equation applies to the propagation of a single photon, or the propagation of an ensemble of indistinguishable photons, and enables the accurate prediction of measured {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric patterns continuously from the near to the far field.<ref name="D1993"/><ref name="D2004"/> Interferograms generated with this equation have been shown to compare well with measured interferograms for both even ({{math|''N'' {{=}} 2, 4, 6...}}) and odd ({{math|''N'' {{=}} 3, 5, 7...}}) values of {{mvar|N}} from 2 to 1600.<ref name="D1993"/><ref name="D2003">{{cite book|author-link=F. J. Duarte |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |title=Tunable Laser Optics |edition=2nd |publisher=CRC |location=New York, NY |date=2015 |isbn=978-1-4822-4529-5}}{{page needed|date=October 2017}}</ref>

==Applications==
At a practical level, the {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric equation was introduced for imaging applications<ref name="D1993"/> and is routinely applied to predict {{mvar|N}}-slit laser interferograms, both in the near and far field. Thus, it has become a valuable tool in the alignment of large, and very large, {{mvar|N}}-slit laser interferometers<ref name=JOPT2010>{{cite journal |first1=F. J. |last1=Duarte |first2=T. S. |last2=Taylor |first3=A. B. |last3=Clark |first4=W. E. |last4=Davenport |title=The {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometer: an extended configuration |journal=J. Opt. |volume=12 |issue=1 |article-number=015705 |date=2010 |doi=10.1088/2040-8978/12/1/015705|bibcode=2010JOpt...12a5705D |s2cid=121521124 }}</ref><ref name = JOPT2011>{{cite journal |first1=F. J. |last1=Duarte |first2=T. S. |last2=Taylor |first3=A. M. |last3=Black |first4=W. E. |last4=Davenport |first5=P. G. |last5=Varmette |title={{mvar|N}}-slit interferometer for secure free-space optical communications: 527&nbsp;m intra interferometric path length |journal=J. Opt. |volume=13 |article-number=035710 |date=2011 |issue=3 |doi=10.1088/2040-8978/13/3/035710 |bibcode=2011JOpt...13c5710D|s2cid=6086533 }}</ref> used in the study of clear air turbulence and the propagation of ''interferometric characters'' for [[Laser communication in space|secure laser communications in space]]. Other analytical applications are described below.

[[File:FJDUARTE-LASERS-JOPT13-035710(2011).jpg|170px|thumb|right|Interferogram for {{math|''N'' {{=}} 3}} slits with diffraction pattern superimposed on the right outer wing.<ref name = JOPT2011 />]]

===Generalized diffraction and refraction===
The {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric equation has been applied to describe classical phenomena such as [[interference (wave propagation)|interference]], [[diffraction]], [[refraction]] ([[Snell's law]]), and [[Reflection (physics)|reflection]], in a rational and unified approach, using quantum mechanics principles.<ref name="D2003"/><ref name="D1997">{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |title=Interference, diffraction, and refraction, via Dirac's notation |journal=Am. J. Phys. |volume=65 |issue=7 |pages=637–640 |date=1997 |doi=10.1119/1.18613 |bibcode=1997AmJPh..65..637D}}</ref> In particular, this interferometric approach has been used to derive generalized refraction equations for both positive and [[negative refraction]],<ref name=APB>{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |title=Multiple-prism dispersion equations for positive and negative refraction |journal=Appl. Phys. B |volume=82 |issue=1 |pages=35–38 |date=2006 |doi=10.1007/s00340-005-1996-x |bibcode=2006ApPhB..82...35D|s2cid=120462686 }}</ref> thus providing a clear link between diffraction theory and generalized refraction.<ref name=APB />

From the phase term, of the interferometric equation, the expression

:<math> d_m \left(\pm n_1 \sin{\theta_m} \pm n_2 \sin{\phi_m} \right) \left(\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\right)= M \pi</math>

can be obtained, where {{math|''M'' {{=}} 0, 2, 4...}}.

For {{math|''n''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} ''n''<sub>2</sub>}}, this equation can be written as<ref name="D2003"/><ref name="D1997"/>

:<math> d_m \left(\pm \sin{\theta_m} \pm \sin{\phi_m} \right) = m \lambda</math>

which is the generalized diffraction [[grating equation]]. Here, {{mvar|θ<sub>m</sub>}} is the angle of incidence, {{mvar|φ<sub>m</sub>}} is the angle of diffraction, {{mvar|λ}} is the wavelength, and {{math|''m'' {{=}} 0, 1, 2...}} is the order of diffraction.

Under certain conditions, {{math|''d<sub>m</sub>'' ≪ ''λ''}}, which can be readily obtained experimentally, the phase term becomes<ref name="D2003"/><ref name="D1997"/>

:<math>\left(\pm n_1 \sin{\theta_m} \pm n_2 \sin{\phi_m} \right) = 0</math>

which is the generalized refraction equation,<ref name="APB" /> where {{mvar|θ<sub>m</sub>}} is the angle of incidence, and {{mvar|φ<sub>m</sub>}} now becomes the angle of refraction.

===Cavity linewidth equation===
Furthermore, the {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric equation has been applied to derive the [[laser linewidth|cavity linewidth equation]] applicable to dispersive oscillators, such as the [[multiple-prism grating laser oscillators]]:<ref>{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |title=Cavity dispersion equation: a note on its origin |journal=Appl. Opt. |volume=31 |issue=33 |pages=6979–6982 |date=1992 |doi=10.1364/AO.31.006979 |pmid=20802556 |bibcode=1992ApOpt..31.6979D}}</ref>

:<math> \Delta\lambda \approx \Delta \theta \left(\frac{\partial\Theta}{\partial\lambda}\right)^{-1}</math>

In this equation, {{math|Δ''θ''}} is the beam divergence and the overall intracavity angular dispersion is the quantity in parentheses.

===Fourier transform imaging===
Researchers working on Fourier-transform ghost imaging consider the {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric equation<ref name="D1989"/><ref name="D1993"/><ref name="D1997"/> as an avenue to investigate the quantum nature of ghost imaging.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=H. |last1=Liu |first2=X. |last2=Shen |first3=D.-M. |last3=Zhu |first4=S. |last4=Han |title=Fourier-transform ghost imaging with pure far-field correlated thermal light |journal=Phys. Rev. A |volume=76 |issue=5 |article-number=053808 |date=2007 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.76.053808 |bibcode=2007PhRvA..76e3808L}}</ref> Also, the {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric approach is one of several approaches applied to describe basic optical phenomena in a cohesive and unified manner.<ref>{{cite journal |first=J. |last=Kurusingal |title=Law of normal scattering – a comprehensive law for wave propagation at an interface |journal=J. Opt. Soc. Am. A |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=98–108 |date=2007 |doi=10.1364/JOSAA.24.000098 |pmid=17164848 |bibcode=2007JOSAA..24...98K}}</ref>

Note: given the various terminologies in use, for {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometry, it should be made explicit that the {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric equation applies to two-slit interference, three-slit interference, four-slit interference, etc.

===Quantum entanglement===
The Dirac principles and probabilistic methodology used to derive the {{mvar|N}}-slit interferometric equation have also been used to derive the polarization [[quantum entanglement]] probability amplitude<ref name=QOE>{{cite book |title=Quantum Optics for Engineers |publisher=CRC |location=New York |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-4398-8853-7 |oclc=871400712 |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |author-link=F. J. Duarte}}</ref>

:<math>\left|\psi\right\rang= \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\bigl(\left|x\right\rang_{1} \left|y\right\rang_{2}- \left|y\right\rang_{1} \left|x\right\rang_{2}\bigr) </math>

and corresponding probability amplitudes depicting the propagation of multiple pairs of quanta.<ref>{{cite journal |first=F. J. |last=Duarte |title=Secure space-to-space interferometric communications and its nexus to the physics of quantum entanglement |journal=Appl. Phys. Rev. |volume=3 |issue=4 |article-number=041301 |date=2016 |doi=10.1063/1.4966139 |bibcode=2016ApPRv...3d1301D}}</ref>

==Comparison with classical methods==
A comparison of the Dirac approach with classical methods, in the performance of interferometric calculations, has been done by [[Travis S. Taylor]] ''et al''.<ref>{{cite book |first=T. S. |last=Taylor |display-authors=etal |contribution=Comparison of Fourier and Dirac calculations for classical optics |title=Proceedings of the International Conference on Lasers '95 |publisher=STS |location=McLean, VA |date=1996 |pages=487–492}}</ref> These authors concluded that the interferometric equation, derived via the Dirac formalism, was advantageous in the very near field.

Some differences between the DD interferometric equation and classical formalisms can be summarized as follows:

* The classical Fresnel approach is used for near-field applications and the classical Fraunhofer approach is used for far-field applications. That division is not necessary when using the DD interferometric approach as this formalism applies to both the near and the far-field cases.<ref name="D1993"/>
* The Fraunhofer approach works for plane-wave illumination.<ref>{{cite book |first=G. R. |last=Fowles |title=Introduction to Modern Optics |publisher=[[Holt, Rinehart and Winston]] |location=New York, NY |date=1968}}{{page needed|date=October 2017}}</ref> The DD approach works for both, plane wave illumination or highly diffractive illumination patterns.<ref name="D1993"/>
* The DD interferometric equation is statistical in character. This is not the case of the classical formulations.

So far there has been no published comparison with more general classical approaches based on the [[Huygens–Fresnel principle]] or [[Kirchhoff's diffraction formula]].
